bites.title: Specialist agents (researcher, writer, editor)
bites.body:
A classic multi-agent pattern divides a complex content or analysis job across three distinct roles: a researcher, a writer and an editor.

The researcher has search and database tools, and its only job is to gather verified facts and source citations. The writer has no search tools; it takes the researcher's notes and turns them into a clear draft that follows the style guide. The editor checks the draft against the source notes and the client rubric.

It is how a newspaper works: reporters gather the facts, feature writers craft the piece and sub-editors check accuracy and house style.

Each prompt stays short and focused on one skill instead of juggling three at once.
bites.sourceNote: Drafted by AI, November 2026 · confidence: high

questions.prompt: Why does separating researcher, writer and editor roles often beat a single all-in-one prompt?

choices.text: Three agents always cost a third of the tokens of one agent
Each agent focuses on one clear objective with its own tailored prompt and tools, reducing conflicting instructions
The writer can invent facts freely without the editor checking them
None of the agents need to read the user's request

questions.explanation: Splitting gathering, drafting and checking keeps each prompt focused and lets the editor audit the writer against the researcher's facts.

bites.title: Applying single responsibility to teams
bites.body:
In software engineering, the single-responsibility principle says each module should have one clear job and one reason to change. The same rule applies to agent teams.

When one agent is responsible for SQL queries, policy interpretation, customer tone and refund approval, tweaking the prompt to fix a SQL bug often breaks the customer tone. When each agent has a single responsibility, you can improve and test the SQL agent without touching the customer-service writer.

It is keeping the kitchen separate from the front-of-house staff so changing the oven does not muddle the table bookings.

Give each agent one clear job whose output you can test on its own.
bites.sourceNote: Drafted by AI, November 2026 · confidence: high

questions.prompt: How does the single-responsibility principle help when maintaining a multi-agent system?

choices.text: It forces all agents to share a single giant system prompt
It means the whole team can only answer one question per day
You can improve and test one specialist agent's prompt or tools without accidentally breaking unrelated behaviours
It removes the need for any evaluation tests

questions.explanation: Narrow, well-bounded responsibilities make individual agents much easier to tune, test and debug in isolation.

bites.title: Start from the work, not the org chart: list the tasks first
bites.body:
A common mistake when building a multi-agent system is starting by inventing a grand company org chart: a CEO agent, a VP of Strategy agent, a Marketing Director agent and an Intern agent.

Models do not need middle management. Start instead by listing the concrete tasks required to turn the input into the output, the tools each task needs and the checks between them. Only group tasks into separate agents when they genuinely need different tools, different context or an independent review perspective.

It is designing a workshop around the machines and steps needed to build a chair, not hiring five vice-presidents first.

If two agents have the same tools and run back-to-back on the same context, they should almost certainly be one agent.
bites.sourceNote: Drafted by AI, November 2026 · confidence: high

questions.prompt: What is the right way to decide which agents a team needs?

choices.text: Copy the client's human organisation chart including every middle-management layer
Always create exactly ten agents for every project
List the concrete tasks, tools and checks first, and create separate agents only where tools, context or review roles differ
Create one agent per word in the user's prompt

questions.explanation: Agent boundaries should follow real differences in tools, context isolation or verification, not human job titles.

bites.title: Each agent gets only the tools its job needs
bites.body:
If your system has twenty tools in total and you hand all twenty to every agent in the team, every agent pays the token cost of twenty tool definitions and risks calling a tool it has no business touching.

Scope tools strictly per agent. Give the research agent the read-only search and database lookup tools. Give the writer agent no external tools at all. Give the action agent the email or CRM-update tool only after the approval step has passed.

It is hotel keycards: the cleaner's card opens the linen cupboards, the guest's card opens Room 304, and only the duty manager's card opens the safe.

Least-privilege tool access improves both accuracy and security.
bites.sourceNote: Drafted by AI, November 2026 · confidence: high

questions.prompt: Why should each agent in a team receive only the tools required for its specific role?

choices.text: Models refuse to run if they see more than two tools
It reduces tool-selection mistakes, saves prompt tokens and prevents an agent from taking actions outside its remit
Giving every agent every tool makes the system safer
Tool definitions do not use any context tokens

questions.explanation: Scoping tools per agent applies least privilege, shrinks prompts and keeps each specialist focused on the right actions.

bites.title: A reviewer agent that checks work before it leaves the team
bites.body:
Before a multi-agent team hands its final output to the user or triggers an external action, a dedicated reviewer step acts as the quality gate at the door.

The reviewer agent does not write content from scratch. It checks the candidate output against a strict checklist: are all claims supported by the research notes, are any confidential fields leaked, does the JSON match the schema, and was every part of the user's question answered?

It is the dispatch inspector at a factory who checks the finished product against the order sheet before the box is sealed.

Combine deterministic code checks with the reviewer agent so mechanical rules are checked by code and judgement rules by the model.
bites.sourceNote: Drafted by AI, November 2026 · confidence: high

questions.prompt: What is the role of a reviewer agent at the end of a team workflow?

choices.text: To audit the draft output against accuracy, safety and completeness criteria before it reaches the user
To rewrite the user's original question so it matches the wrong answer
To delete all source citations from the report
To run before any research or drafting has started

questions.explanation: A final reviewer acts as an internal quality gate, catching unsupported claims or missed requirements before delivery.

bites.title: The smallest team that passes your evals
bites.body:
Every extra agent you add to a team introduces another prompt to maintain, another handoff that can lose nuance, more latency and higher token bills.

Treat team size as a cost to minimise, not a badge of sophistication. Build your evaluation suite first. Try a single well-prompted agent with good tools. Add a second agent (such as a verifier or a specialist) only if your eval scores prove that the extra agent fixes a real failure mode that one agent could not handle.

It is hiring staff for a small shop: you bring in a second person when the queue out the door proves one person cannot keep up.

The best team is the smallest one that passes your evals reliably.
bites.sourceNote: Drafted by AI, November 2026 · confidence: high

questions.prompt: How should you decide whether to add another agent to your system?

choices.text: Add more agents whenever you want the architecture diagram to look impressive
Always start with at least eight agents before writing any tests
Only add an agent when your evaluations show it solves a failure mode that a simpler setup cannot
Add an agent every time a prompt has a spelling mistake

questions.explanation: Every additional agent adds latency, cost and handoff risk, so justify each one with measured gains on your eval suite.
